articles.headline: Treasury Sanctions Iranian Shadow Banking Networks in 'Operation Economic Outcast'
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has designated over two dozen Iranian exchange houses, front companies, and key personnel as part of 'Operation Economic Outcast.' This sweeping action aims to disrupt Iran's global shadow banking networks, which are used to facilitate Iranian oil sales and move billions of dollars in proceeds for the regime.

The designations target the financial infrastructure underpinning much of Iran's remaining foreign trade, including exchange houses, bank-affiliated 'rahbar' companies, and overseas front companies in the UAE, Hong Kong, and Turkey. These entities are accused of enabling Iran to access foreign currency despite comprehensive sanctions and of enriching themselves by diverting state resources.

This action was taken under Executive Orders 13902, 13224, and 13871, which target specific sectors of the Iranian economy, counter-terrorism, and the metals industry, respectively. Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent stated that Iran's shadow banking system is the 'last financial lifeline of a bankrupt regime' and vowed to continue dismantling these illicit networks.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Iran Designations and New Cuba Sanctions FAQs
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran designations and issued Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) related to Cuba sanctions. The Iran designations are part of ongoing efforts to target the regime's financial networks.

The Cuba-related FAQs, specifically 1277 and 1278, clarify that OFAC's sanctions authority covering Cuba's manufacturing, technology, electronics, and marine sectors does not automatically sanction all persons operating in those sectors. The guidance also confirms that authorized activities involving Cuba's marine sector, including payments to Cuban ports for authorized trade and certain humanitarian transactions, may continue.

These clarifications come after Washington expanded its sanctions on November 5, 2026, to include foreign firms operating in Cuba's electronics, manufacturing, marine, or technology sectors, making them liable to U.S. sanctions.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Counter Narcotics and Cyber Designations, Amends Russia-Related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new counter narcotics and cyber-related designations. Concurrently, OFAC issued Illicit Drugs General License 1, authorizing the wind down of transactions involving certain persons blocked on November 19, 2026.

Additionally, OFAC issued Russia-related General License 131L, which authorizes certain transactions related to negotiating and entering into contingent contracts for the sale of Lukoil International GmbH, along with related maintenance activities. This action also included amendments to associated Russia-related FAQs 1224 and 1225.

Among the individuals added to OFAC's SDN List under counter narcotics authorities are Marco Francis Coffen, Francesco Commisso, Rocco Remo Commisso, Vincenzo Demaria, and Angelo Figliomeni, linked to various organized crime groups. An entity, Bei Fang Bo Lin Construction Decoration Co., Ltd., was also added.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Hizballah-Linked Charity and Gold Smuggling Network
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has imposed counter-terrorism designations targeting a Lebanon-based charity, its founder, and members of a Lebanon- and Türkiye-based gold and cash smuggling network. These actions are part of an ongoing effort to disrupt financial channels supporting Hizballah and Iran's IRGC-Qods Force.

The designated charity, Wa Ta'awanu Association, and its founder, Afif Abdel Rida Chouman, are accused of supporting Hizballah under the guise of humanitarian assistance. OFAC alleges that the association channels donor funds towards Hizballah's activities and provides cover for its operations.

Additionally, OFAC designated individuals Hassan Khechen and Ibrahim Khechen, along with entities Gold Global Company (Lebanon) and Sankari Gold Kuyumculuk Ticaret Limited Sirketi (Turkey), for their involvement in a gold and cash smuggling network tied to Hizballah. These designations expose the groups to asset freezes and secondary sanctions.

articles.headline: OFAC Sanctions Guatemalan Drug Trafficking Organizations Supporting Mexican Cartels
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has designated two Guatemalan drug trafficking organizations, Los Lorenzanas and Los Mendoza Drug Trafficking Organization, under counter narcotics and counter terrorism authorities. These groups are sanctioned for their support of Mexican narco-terrorist cartels, including the Sinaloa Cartel and Cartel de Jalisco Nueva Generacion (CJNG).

Los Lorenzanas has been designated as a Foreign Terrorist Organization (FTO) and a Specially Designated Global Terrorist (SDGT). Los Mendoza Drug Trafficking Organization was sanctioned under Executive Orders 14059 and 13224.

OFAC also updated the listing for Los Huistas Drug Trafficking Organization to include secondary sanctions risk and links to the Sinaloa Cartel and CJNG. These designations result in asset freezes and prohibit U.S. persons from engaging in transactions with the designated entities.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Update to Iran Designation List
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced an update to its Iran designation list. This action reflects ongoing efforts to maintain pressure on the Iranian regime through targeted sanctions.

While specific details of the update were not immediately released in a separate press statement, such actions typically involve adding or modifying entries on the Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) List. These updates aim to further disrupt financial networks and activities that support the Iranian government.
The U.S. Department of the Treasury continues to utilize its sanctions authorities to address the national emergency posed by Iran, with a focus on severing the regime's remaining economic lifelines.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes New Iran-Related Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new Iran-related designations. These actions are part of the broader 'Operation Economic Outcast,' which aims to cripple financial networks sustaining the Iranian regime.

The designations target individuals and entities involved in facilitating illicit financial activities for Iran. This ongoing pressure seeks to disrupt the regime's ability to generate revenue and fund its destabilizing activities.
The U.S. government has consistently stated its commitment to using sanctions as a tool to address Iran's behavior, including its support for terrorism and its nuclear program.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Cuban Entities and Expands Sanctions to Key Economic Sectors
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new cyber-related and transnational criminal organizations designations, alongside significant Cuba designations and the publication of a Cuba-related determination. On November 5, 2026, the U.S. government made foreign firms operating in Cuba's electronics, manufacturing, marine, or technology sectors liable to U.S. sanctions.

This action designated eight companies and two individuals, and identified five tankers as blocked property, linking them to Cuba's fuel shipping, state companies, ruling elite, and military supply. The determination extends a provision of Executive Order 14404 of May 1, 2026, which authorizes sanctions on foreign persons found to operate in specific sectors of the Cuban economy.

Among the designated entities are Chinese state-linked companies, China National Electronic Import and Export Company (CEIEC) and Beijing H&C Technologies Co., Ltd., for their work with a Cuban arms procurement entity. Cuban state media and Beijing have condemned these new measures, with China asserting its cooperation with Cuba is legitimate.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Iran-Related Designations, Alert, and Amended Venezuela General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new Iran-related designations, updates to certain Iran-related listings, and the publication of an Iran-related OFAC Alert. This action also includes the issuance of an amended Venezuela-related General License and a Frequently Asked Question.

The Iran-related OFAC Alert focuses on the Iranian Shadow Fleet's reliance on false flags for sanctions evasion, highlighting ongoing efforts to circumvent international restrictions. These measures are part of the U.S. strategy to disrupt Iran's illicit oil trade and financial networks.

Regarding Venezuela, OFAC issued General License 5AA, which further delays the effectiveness of the authorization in GL 5 until December 18, 2026. This means that transactions related to the sale or transfer of CITGO shares in connection with the PdVSA 2020 8.5 percent bond remain prohibited unless specifically authorized by OFAC during this period.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends Iran-Related General License for International Development Bank
body: The Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has issued Iran General License FF-1, titled 'Authorizing the Wind Down of Transactions Involving International Development Bank for Investment and Finance.'

This amended general license provides authorization for the wind-down of specific transactions, indicating a targeted adjustment to existing sanctions against Iran. Such licenses are often issued to allow for the orderly cessation of activities that would otherwise be prohibited under sanctions regimes.

The issuance of this general license reflects OFAC's dynamic approach to sanctions implementation, allowing for flexibility in certain circumstances while maintaining overall pressure on designated entities and sectors.

articles.headline: EU Unveils 22nd Sanctions Package Against Russia, Targeting Banks, Crypto, and Sports
body: The European Commission has proposed its 22nd package of sanctions against Russia, aiming to intensify pressure on Moscow over its ongoing conflict in Ukraine. The new measures target approximately 60 additional Russian banks with transaction bans and SWIFT disconnections.

The package also establishes a dedicated Crypto Sanctions Task Force to combat the use of cryptocurrency networks by Russia and third countries to evade restrictions. Furthermore, it expands the energy services ban to include electricity services and proposes a ban on all tanker vessels insured in Russia, alongside listing over 70 more ships linked to Moscow's shadow fleet.

In response to an escalation in 'non-conventional kinetic activities' by Russian operatives, the package activates an EU-wide visa ban on current and former Russian combatants and prohibits EU citizens from serving on the governing boards of Russian companies. It also bans Russian teams and athletes from competing under the Russian flag at EU sporting events and restricts Russian sponsorship flows into European sports and cultural bodies.

articles.headline: Global Markets React to Escalating Geopolitical Tensions and Sanctions
body: Global financial markets are showing increased volatility as investors react to escalating geopolitical tensions, particularly the new round of EU sanctions against Russia and ongoing U.S. sanctions on Iran and Cuba. The comprehensive nature of the EU's 22nd sanctions package, targeting Russian banks, cryptocurrency networks, and energy sectors, is expected to have a notable impact on European and global trade flows.

Energy prices are a key concern, with the EU's proposed ban on Russian-insured tanker vessels and expanded energy services restrictions potentially affecting global oil and gas supplies. This comes amidst existing U.S. efforts to disrupt Iran's illicit oil trade, further tightening the supply outlook.

Analysts are closely watching central bank responses, as the combined effect of sanctions and supply chain disruptions could fuel inflation. The increased focus on sanctions evasion, particularly through cryptocurrency and shadow banking networks, also poses new challenges for financial institutions and regulatory bodies worldwide.

articles.headline: UN General Assembly Reaffirms Call for End to US Embargo on Cuba Amidst Worsening Humanitarian Crisis
body: The United Nations General Assembly has once again adopted a resolution calling for the termination of the U.S. embargo against Cuba, a position it has reaffirmed almost every year since 1992. This comes as Cuba faces a severe humanitarian crisis, exacerbated by six decades of unilateral coercive measures by the United States.

The U.S. fuel blockade, implemented in January 2026, has significantly worsened the situation, deterring third countries from supplying oil and fuel to Cuba and leading to severe social and economic hardships for ordinary Cubans. The blockade has created immense difficulties in obtaining essential goods, including medicines and medical equipment.

Cuba's financial exclusion from the international banking system, due to fears of violating U.S. sanctions, has made it exceptionally difficult to process payments and engage in trade, even for humanitarian purposes. The UN Special Rapporteur on Unilateral Coercive Measures has highlighted the severe detriment these actions inflict on basic human rights.

articles.headline: OCC Issues New Guidance on Managing Third-Party Risk for Financial Institutions
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) has issued new guidance for financial institutions on managing risks associated with third-party relationships. This guidance emphasizes the importance of robust risk management frameworks for activities conducted through third parties, including fintech partnerships and cloud service providers.

The OCC's advisory highlights key areas of concern such as due diligence, contract negotiation, ongoing monitoring, and termination processes. It stresses that banks remain responsible for managing risks even when activities are outsourced, and that inadequate oversight can lead to significant operational, compliance, and reputational risks.

This guidance aims to ensure that national banks and federal savings associations effectively identify, assess, and mitigate risks across their third-party ecosystems, particularly as financial services become increasingly reliant on external vendors and technology solutions.

articles.headline: BIS Imposes New Export Controls on Remote Access to Advanced AI Chips and Overseas Data Centers
body: The U.S. Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) has issued an interim final rule (IFR) expanding export controls related to advanced computing items, including advanced semiconductors and certain foreign data center activities. Published in the Federal Register on November 19, 2026, the rule aims to prevent circumvention of existing restrictions on U.S. computing chips through remote computing arrangements, such as cloud services offered by data centers in third countries.

The IFR establishes new licensing requirements for exports, reexports, or in-country transfers of advanced computing items if there is 'knowledge' that the item is destined for a data center providing access to a 'significant volume of compute power' (over 12 million aggregate TPP) to end users headquartered in Macau or a Country Group D:5 destination, including China. This imposes significant 'know your customer' (KYC) obligations on exporters and data center operators.

Additionally, the rule imposes a new destination-based license requirement for advanced computing items to or within Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Brazil, which BIS views as presenting a higher-than-normal risk of diversion. The IFR also formally rescinds the Biden-era AI Diffusion Rule and tightens rules for chip foundries and packagers.

articles.headline: Department of State Adds Four Cuban State-Owned Enterprises to Entity List
body: The U.S. Department of State has added four Cuban state-owned enterprises to the Entity List, effective September 17, 2026, as published in the Federal Register on November 24, 2026. These entities are designated pursuant to Section 2(a)(i)(A) of Executive Order 14404 for operating in or having operated in the metals and mining sector of the Cuban economy.

The designated entities include EMPRESA DE SERVICIOS TECNICOS DE COMPUTACION COMUNICACIONES Y ELECTRONICA (SERCONI), EMPRESA DE INGENIERIA Y PROYECTOS DEL NIQUEL (CEPRONIQUEL), CENTRO DE INVESTIGACIONES DEL NIQUEL CAPITAN ALBERTO FERNANDEZ MONTES DE OCA (CEDINIQ), and PINARES S.A. All are located in Moa, Holguin, Cuba, and are involved in support activities for mining and quarrying.

As a result of these designations, all property and interests in property subject to U.S. jurisdiction of these persons are blocked. This action further expands U.S. sanctions targeting key sectors of the Cuban economy under Executive Order 14404, which was issued on May 1, 2026.
articles.source: Federal Register / U.S. Department of State

articles.headline: Addressing Remote Access to Advanced Semiconductors
body: In this interim final rule (IFR), the Department of Commerce is establishing new rules to prevent certain foreign actors from leveraging advanced computing power based on U.S. technology to threaten U.S. national security and foreign policy interests. First, this rule establishes new restrictions which will apply for exports, reexports, or transfers (in-country) to overseas data centers that remotely supply significant volumes of compute to companies headquartered in Country Group D:5 or Macau. These restrictions will undermine the ability of companies headquartered in countries of concern from using U.S. advanced Super Intelligence (SI) semiconductors to train advanced SI models. Data centers, foreign foundries, and chip exporters are required to perform robust due diligence on their customers, including any direct or indirect ownership or control by persons in Country Group D:5 or Macau, as part of complying with this new control. The license requirement will not apply to commercial recommender systems, such as those used by online retailers or social media companies, as these functions do not pose the same national security threat. Second, in addition to the current license requirements for advanced semiconductors, a license will be required to export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) advanced semiconductors to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, or Brazil (and any additional country designated by the Secretary of Commerce, in consultation with the Secretary of State or the Assistant to the President for National Security Affairs)--countries which present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion. The license requirement for these five countries will not apply to semiconductors destined to companies headquartered in, or whose ultimate parent company is headquartered in, the United States, provided certain reporting requirements are met. Commerce will be actively monitoring for countries that tolerate evasion of this IFR and will consider a range of consequences for such countries, such as import restrictions, new license requirements on advanced semiconductor exports, downgrading the country's status in the U.S. export control regime, and Entity List designations and temporary export prohibitions for foreign persons involved in such activities. Third, this IFR amends the presumptions which front-end chips fabricators and chip packagers face when exporting advanced-node logic chips. These amendments reduce the number of pathways to overcome the presumptions for chip designers located in destinations which face a license requirement for SI chips. This change gives the U.S. government critical oversight over companies headquartered in certain countries that seek to leverage advanced semiconductor production capabilities in third countries. Finally, the IFR formally rescinds the regulations implementing the Biden-era AI Diffusion Rule. The AI Diffusion Rule has never been enforced. The regulatory changes in this rule formalize the rescission of the AI Diffusion Rule, which the Department of Commerce Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) announced in May 2025.

articles.headline: Extension of the Suspension of Expansion of End-User Controls for Affiliates of Certain Listed Entities
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is extending the suspension of the interim final rule (IFR), "Expansion of End-User Controls to Cover Affiliates of Certain Listed Entities." The suspension was set to end November 9, 2026. This final rule extends the suspension through January 10, 2027.

articles.headline: Revisions to the Entity List
body: In this rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) revises the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by removing two addresses associated with Arrow Electronics (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd. from the Entity List under the destination of China, People's Republic of (China). This determination follows the removal from the Entity List of Arrow China Electronics Trading Co., Ltd., and the removal of six aliases for Arrow Electronics (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd. in November 2025.

articles.headline: Removal From the Entity List
body: In this rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by removing one entity from the Entity List under the destination of Turkey.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.
